story: Before writing the beloved masterpiece 'The Little Prince', French aristocratic aviator Antoine de Saint-Exupéry faced a desperate battle for survival in the Sahara Desert. In December 1935, during a high-speed air race, Saint-Exupéry and his mechanic-navigator, André Prévot, crashed their Caudron Simoun aircraft into the Libyan sands. Stranded with almost no food or water, they spent four agonizing days battling severe dehydration and nearing the brink of death. Just as hope faded, a Bedouin traveler miraculously appeared, saving their lives with the gift of water. This harrowing experience inspired Saint-Exupéry's award-winning memoir 'Wind, Sand and Stars' and the desert setting of 'The Little Prince'. Decades later, Saint-Exupéry's life ended in another skyward mystery when his P-38 reconnaissance plane vanished over the Mediterranean in 1944, leaving a legacy of a twin innocent who, like his little prince, fell from the sky.
angle: Before writing 'The Little Prince', Antoine de Saint-Exupéry nearly died of thirst in the Sahara Desert after a crash, only to be miraculously saved by a passing Bedouin.

claims.claim: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry was a French aristocrat, writer, and pioneering aviator.
In December 1935, Saint-Exupéry and his navigator André Prévot crashed their plane in the Sahara Desert.
The crash survivors were stranded with almost no water or food and faced extreme dehydration.
They were rescued after several days by a Bedouin who gave them water.
The crash and rescue inspired Saint-Exupéry's 1939 memoir 'Wind, Sand and Stars' (titled 'Terre des hommes' in French).
'Wind, Sand and Stars' won the U.S. National Book Award.
The desert crash also inspired the setting of Saint-Exupéry's famous 1943 children's book 'The Little Prince'.
On July 31, 1944, Saint-Exupéry vanished while flying a Lockheed P-38 Lightning on a WWII military reconnaissance mission.
In September 1998, a fisherman named Jean-Claude Bianco discovered a silver identity bracelet bearing Saint-Exupéry's name off Marseille.
Diver Luc Vanrell located the remains of Saint-Exupéry's downed P-38 Lightning on the ocean floor near Marseille.
Former Luftwaffe pilot Horst Rippert claimed decades later that he was the pilot who shot down Saint-Exupéry.
Rippert expressed deep regret because he had read and idolized Saint-Exupéry's books in his youth.
Investigators who examined the recovered P-38 wreckage found no bullet holes or combat damage.
Saint-Exupéry was married to Consuelo Suncin, a writer and artist.
The asteroid deflection organization B612 Foundation was named in tribute to the home asteroid of the Little Prince.

disputed: The exact cause of Saint-Exupéry's 1944 crash is disputed. While Horst Rippert claimed he shot down the plane, no German military records survive to verify this, and the plane wreckage shows no bullet holes. Furthermore, some associates suggest Saint-Exupéry may have committed suicide. A script should present Rippert's confession and the suicide theory as unverified hypotheses, concluding that the final cause remains a mystery.
